banter: Mind the rope. It has already caught two tourists and someone from management.
If a gull offers you legal advice, keep walking. They're all involved.
I've survived storms, engine fires, and a company team-building weekend. Only one still gives me nightmares.
The mug says captain. Payroll prefers a less expensive interpretation.
You have questions. I have coffee. Let's see which runs out first.
Don't lean on that crate. It's either expensive equipment or a very confident rat.
The sea keeps its secrets. This harbor puts them on an invoice.
I used to trust people. Then someone invented the phrase 'water-resistant luggage'.
I'm not superstitious. I just respect the possibility that the boat holds grudges.
If you're here about the missing sandwich, I can identify the gull.

london: They asked about meeting someone beside the Thames. I told them to specify a bank. Apparently that was 'unhelpful nautical aggression'.
They had marked the Thames on a map and asked where to find a quiet stretch in the capital. Then they asked about somewhere near the clock tower. Pick a strategy.
They wanted a riverside meeting along the Thames, near the buildings where politicians argue. I suggested bringing enough food for a long wait.
They asked whether the Thames would make a good escape route. I said that depended on the boat. They seemed disappointed that a boat was necessary.
paris: They were studying bridges over the Seine. Not the architecture. More the number of ways to leave in a hurry.
They asked about a meeting beside the Seine, with an iron tower somewhere in view. Apparently a normal street corner lacked atmosphere.
They wanted to know about boats on the Seine. Then they asked whether passengers could keep a large parcel beside them. Romantic, in a customs violation sort of way.
They mentioned a capital on the Seine and asked if river cruises attracted much attention. Only from everyone holding a camera.
berlin: They pointed to the Spree and asked about boats in the capital. I said inland water still counts. Some people need that explained.
They wanted to meet someone beside the Spree, in the city with the famous former Wall. Apparently ordinary walls weren't specific enough.
They asked about the Spree and the Havel. Two waterways, one very nervous traveler, and absolutely no interest in fishing.
Their next stop was a capital on the Spree. They asked if arriving by water would look unusual. Less unusual than asking me that four times.
new_york_city: They asked about the Hudson and a harbor with a woman holding a torch. I said she probably wasn't their contact.
They wanted the city beside the Hudson, the one with the skyline that looks like a shipping manifest standing on end.
They asked whether a waterfront meeting near Manhattan would be discreet. I suggested removing the word Manhattan from that plan.
They had circled the Hudson on their map and drawn a tiny torch beside the harbor. Terrible drawing. Useful directions.
warsaw: They asked about the capital on the Vistula. I said a river that long deserved a shorter interrogation.
They wanted a meeting beside the Vistula, in the capital with the mermaid. Finally, directions with someone from my line of work.
They were heading to a capital on the river called Wisla locally. Wrote down both names, then asked if that counted as two rivers.
They mentioned the Vistula and a rebuilt old town. Asked if the waterfront was a good place to disappear. I told them to start by not announcing it.
new_delhi: They asked about the Yamuna in India's capital. I told them a river on a map wasn't a ferry reservation.
They had marked India's capital and the Yamuna, then asked about a riverside meeting. No fishing rod. Very large suitcase.
They wanted to know whether the Yamuna went straight to the sea. It joins the Ganges instead. Even rivers sometimes need a connection.
They mentioned India's capital and the Yamuna, then asked whether I knew anyone there with a boat. Apparently 'sailor' means international boat directory now.
toronto: They asked about a Canadian city on Lake Ontario. Thought a harbor meant salt water. I nearly confiscated their map.
They wanted the Canadian lakeside city with the very tall tower. Lake Ontario, not the ocean. The water has enough problems without identity theft.
They asked about the harbor on Lake Ontario beneath that needle of a tower. I said the tower wasn't a lighthouse, before they could embarrass us both.
They were heading to a Canadian city on Lake Ontario and asked if the far shore was America. Suddenly geography became very important to them.
kotte: They asked about Diyawanna Lake, where Sri Lanka keeps its parliament on an island. I respect a country that puts water between itself and a committee.
They had circled Parliament Lake near Colombo. Wanted to know whether the parliament really stood on an island. Yes. No, I wouldn't lend them a boat.
They mentioned Sri Lanka's administrative capital and a lake called Diyawanna. Asked for somewhere quiet near parliament. I said to try a day without speeches.
They wanted to meet someone by the lake surrounding Sri Lanka's parliament. They asked if a briefcase would look suspicious. In that neighborhood? They'd blend in.
islamabad: They asked about Rawal Lake, the reservoir serving Pakistan's capital and Rawalpindi. Wanted somewhere by the water. Didn't care about the water. Suspicious attitude.
They had circled Rawal Lake near Pakistan's capital. Asked if it was natural. Artificial reservoir. Their interest in boating sounded artificial too.
They mentioned a capital near Rawal Lake, with the Margalla Hills nearby. Wanted a peaceful meeting. People only specify peaceful when they've considered the alternative.
They asked about the Korang River and Rawal reservoir near Pakistan's capital. That's a lot of homework for someone who claimed to hate geography.
nairobi: They mentioned Kenya's capital and a river with the same name as the city. Convenient. Even I could label that map before coffee.
They asked about the river running through Kenya's capital. No sea voyage involved. Apparently I also provide inland emotional support.
Their next stop was Kenya's capital. They asked about its namesake river, then folded the map before I could recommend a perfectly good coastline.
They wanted a meeting near the river sharing its name with Kenya's capital. I suggested agreeing on a bridge. They said that was too specific. Can't help everyone.
tokyo: They asked about the Sumida, running through Japan's capital toward the bay. Finally, someone who knew rivers had destinations too.
They were interested in boats from Asakusa along the Sumida. Said they liked sightseeing. Never asked about a single sight.
They mentioned the Sumida and a water bus in Japan's capital. I said a bus that floats was a boat with a marketing department.
They had marked the Sumida and the bay beside Japan's capital. Asked whether a boat ride would clear their head. Depends what was bothering their conscience.

repeatLines: The tide has changed. My answer hasn't.
Going in circles is a boat problem, not an investigation strategy.
Unless you're investigating who stole my sandwich. Then arrest the gull.
Asking again won't make their directions any better.
I could add a sea monster, but your paperwork would suffer.
falseLeadLines: Nobody matching that trail came through here.
Plenty of suspicious luggage. Wrong suspicious luggage.
It happens. Usually to people who ignore maps.
The gulls would have mentioned it. They're dreadful with confidential information.
That traveler wasn't at these docks.
I'd offer you a lead, but all I've got is rope.
Your trail doesn't reach this harbor.
On the bright side, you've discovered water.
